name: F#
year_note: Started in late 2001 as 'Caml.NET' at Microsoft Research Cambridge; a research version 0.1 was released quietly on 4 June 2002, a pre-release of F# 1.0 was announced on 5 January 2005, and the productized F# 2.0 shipped with Visual Studio 2010.
tagline: A functional-first ML for .NET: OCaml's core, pipelines and type inference, plus computation expressions that gave the world async.
summary: F# is a strongly typed, functional-first language in the ML family that runs on .NET and interoperates with C# and the rest of the platform. Its core is OCaml-like — Hindley–Milner type inference, discriminated unions, pattern matching and immutable data — with an indentation-aware syntax, .NET objects and interfaces, and features of its own: the |> pipeline style, active patterns, units of measure, type providers and computation expressions. Its async workflows (2007) were the direct precursor of async/await in C# and many later languages.
history:
Don Syme created F# at Microsoft Research Cambridge after helping design and implement .NET generics, which were themselves meant to make the runtime a good target for typed functional languages. In late 2001 he began a 'Caml.NET' implementing the core of OCaml on .NET, renamed it F# to allow divergence from OCaml, and released a first research version in June 2002. F# 1.0, announced in January 2005, and the releases that followed added .NET class and interface programming, the lightweight indentation syntax, quotations, the F# Interactive REPL and active patterns (2006); in 2007 came async workflows and the general computation-expression notation behind them.

After uptake in finance and within Microsoft, Microsoft productized the language, and F# 2.0 shipped with Visual Studio 2010, including Andrew Kennedy's units of measure. F# 3.0 (2012) added type providers and query expressions. The compiler and core library became open source and cross-platform, and development moved into the open on GitHub with the F# Software Foundation; recent releases added task expressions (F# 6, 2021) and nullable reference types (F# 9, 2024). Many of C#'s later features, including generics, var inference, async/await, tuples and pattern matching, were influenced by F#.
innovations: Asynchronous workflows (async { let! ... }, 2007): the direct ancestor of C#'s async/await
Computation expressions: a general, user-extensible notation for monads, sequences, queries and other computations
Units of measure: dimensional analysis checked and inferred by the type system and erased at runtime
Active patterns: user-defined, extensible patterns (views) in a mainstream language
Type providers (F# 3.0): compile-time generation of types from external schemas and data sources
Popularised the |> pipeline operator as a way to write left-to-right data transformations with type inference

typing.notes: Hindley–Milner inference extended with .NET subtyping and overloading. Mostly nominal, but statically resolved type parameters (member constraints) and anonymous records are structural.

influenced_by.note: Began in 2001–2002 as 'Caml.NET', an implementation of the core of OCaml for .NET; renamed F# to allow it to diverge.
The ML tradition of type inference, polymorphism and pattern matching.
Shares the .NET runtime and libraries with C#; objects, properties and events followed C# 1.0 and query expressions followed C# 3.0's LINQ.
Monads and do-notation informed computation expressions.
MailboxProcessor agents follow Erlang-style message passing.

influenced_by_external.name: Isabelle/ML
influenced_by_external.note: Origin of the |> pipeline operator (Tobias Nipkow, 1994).

influenced_by_external.name: .NET Common Language Runtime
influenced_by_external.note: F#'s target platform; .NET 2.0 generics were designed partly with F# in mind.

structured-control.note: if/then/else, for and while are expressions; there is no break or early return.

recursion.note: Recursive functions are marked with let rec.

exceptions.note: try/with (pattern matching on exceptions) and try/finally; Result types are common for expected errors.

generators.note: Sequence expressions: seq { yield ... } produce lazy IEnumerable sequences.

pattern-matching.note: match on unions, tuples, lists and records, extended by active patterns.

tail-calls.note: The compiler emits .NET tail calls and turns self-recursion into loops.

generics.note: Automatic generalization onto .NET generics; statically resolved type parameters for inline member constraints.

option-types.note: Option and ValueOption; F# types do not admit null, and F# 9 (2024) added nullable reference type checking for .NET interop.

structural-typing.note: Anonymous records and member constraints on inline functions are structural.

interfaces.note: .NET interfaces, implemented in classes or inline with object expressions.

classes.note: Full .NET classes, used mainly for interop and encapsulation.

abstract-data-types.note: Signature files (.fsi) and private representations hide a type's implementation.

modules.note: Modules and namespaces with optional signature files; no OCaml-style functors.

operator-overloading.note: Custom symbolic operators and static member operators on types.

immutability.note: let bindings, records, unions and lists are immutable; mutable must be declared.

list-comprehensions.note: List, array and sequence expressions: [ for x in xs do if x % 2 = 0 then x * x ].

lazy-evaluation.note: lazy values and on-demand seq sequences; evaluation is strict by default.

pointers.note: byrefs, nativeptr and fixed for low-level interop.

async-await.note: async { let! ... } workflows announced in October 2007; task { } expressions (F# 6, 2021) produce .NET Tasks directly.

reflection.note: .NET reflection plus FSharp.Reflection for unions and records; code quotations (<@ ... @>) expose typed ASTs.

compile-time-execution.note: Type providers run code inside the compiler to generate types from schemas and data.

declarative-queries.note: query { for c in db.Customers do where ... select ... } expressions translated to LINQ.

significant-whitespace.note: The 'light' indentation-aware syntax, added in 2006, became the default; the verbose OCaml-style syntax remains available.

milestones.event: Research release 0.1 of 'Caml.NET', renamed F#, at Microsoft Research Cambridge (June)
F# 1.0 pre-release announced (January) and demonstrated at Microsoft Research TechFest
Light indentation syntax, active patterns and F# Interactive
Asynchronous workflows and computation expressions announced; Microsoft commits to productizing F#
F# 2.0 ships with Visual Studio 2010, including units of measure
F# 3.0: type providers and query expressions

trivia: According to Syme, the 'F' stands for both 'Functional' and 'System F'; the community saying is 'F is for Fun'.
The |> pipeline operator most associated with F# first appeared in Isabelle/ML in 1994, named by Tobias Nipkow.

hello.notes: A script needs no entry point; a compiled program uses top-level code in its last file or an [<EntryPoint>] function.

factorial.notes: let rec marks a recursive binding; the type int -> int is inferred. int is 32-bit, so larger inputs would use bigint (10I).

fizzbuzz.code:
let fizzbuzz n =
    match n % 3, n % 5 with
    | 0, 0 -> "FizzBuzz"
    | 0, _ -> "Fizz"
    | _, 0 -> "Buzz"
    | _ -> string n

[ 1 .. 15 ] |> List.iter (fizzbuzz >> printfn "%s")
fizzbuzz.expected_output:
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz
fizzbuzz.notes: Matching on a tuple of remainders; >> composes fizzbuzz with printfn.

higher-order.code:
[ 1 .. 10 ]
|> List.filter (fun x -> x % 2 = 0)
|> List.map (fun x -> x * x)
|> List.map string
|> String.concat " "
|> printfn "%s"
higher-order.notes: Pipelines read left to right and let type inference flow along them. A list expression [ for x in 1 .. 10 do if x % 2 = 0 then x * x ] is equivalent.

shapes.code:
// A discriminated union: one type, two cases, each with its own data.
type Shape =
    | Rectangle of width: int * height: int
    | Triangle of baseLength: int * height: int

let area = function
    | Rectangle (w, h) -> w * h
    | Triangle (b, h) -> b * h / 2

printfn "Rectangle: %d" (area (Rectangle (3, 4)))
printfn "Triangle: %d" (area (Triangle (10, 3)))
shapes.notes: A discriminated union with named fields ('base' is a keyword, hence baseLength); function defines a lambda that matches its argument, and the compiler warns about unhandled cases.

signature.title: Computation expressions: async and your own
signature.notes: A user-defined builder turns let! into Bind calls, giving an Option 'maybe' workflow; the same notation drives the built-in async workflow.

toolchains.name: .NET SDK (F# Interactive)
toolchains.notes: The file must end in .fsx. Set DOTNET_NOLOGO=1 and DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1 to silence first-run messages; each run takes a few seconds to start.

browser.name: Fable REPL
browser.notes: Fable compiles F# to JavaScript in the browser; .NET-specific APIs such as Async.Parallel may behave differently or be missing.

runtime.notes: The host's dotnet fsi (SDK 10.0.112) gave identical output.
